text: By July I will have saved enough for the flights.
We will not have finished the itinerary by Friday.
By the time we land, we will have been in the air for twenty-six hours.
Will you have booked the hostel by then?
So you are going in July. Have you booked anything, or is it still a list on your phone?
Still a list. But by the end of this month I will have booked the flights, and the itinerary is almost finished.
Book them this week. We went in peak season too, and by April half the hostels were fully booked.
That is what my cousin said. The cheap flight is a long-haul one with a seven-hour layover.
Take it. It is horrible, and by the time you get there you will have saved almost a thousand.
And the first day is dead anyway, because of the jet lag. I am not planning anything for it.
Good. Leave one empty afternoon in every city as well. Ours turned into a detour that was better than the museums.
Then here is my deadline. Flights by Sunday, hostels by the end of the month, and by the time we set off I will have paid for all of it myself.
Now that is a plan. Send me the dates and I will tell you what to skip.
By the time you wake up, I will already have packed.

Hi Mark. Last class you put three things in order and defended the order out loud. Today you do something a plan needs and a ranking does not, which is a deadline. Here is the idea. Most of the future you already know how to talk about. I will book the flights tonight. We are flying in July. It is going to be expensive. All of those stand at today and look forward. The future perfect does the opposite. It stands at a point in the future and looks back at what is already finished by then. By the time we land in Tokyo, we will have been in the air for twenty-six hours. The landing has not happened yet, and from that landing I am looking backwards at twenty-six hours that are already over. The form is easy and it never changes. Will have, plus the past participle, for every person. I will have saved, she will have saved, they will have saved. Never will has, and never will have save. Now the two traps, and the first one costs a mark in every exam. After by the time, English uses the present, never will. By the time we land, not by the time we will land. The deadline clause is already in the future because the main half says so, and English refuses to say it twice. The second trap is by against until. By is a point, and until is a stretch. I will have booked everything by Friday means finished, Friday at the latest. I will keep looking until Friday means I go on looking right up to Friday and then stop. In Portuguese both of them are ate sexta, and that is exactly why they go wrong. One more thing worth having. Put already inside the sentence for the thing that surprises you. By the time you wake up, I will already have packed. Before class, write four sentences about a trip you have not taken yet, each one starting with by, and put one deadline in every sentence. See you in class, Mark.

Right, voice note, because typing all this would take an hour. So the plan is finally booked and I am telling you now because by the time you read this I will have left. We set off on the fourth of July, which is a Saturday, and the flight is a long-haul one with a four hour layover in Dubai, so by the time we land in Tokyo we will have been traveling for about twenty-six hours and I will be useless for a day. That is the jet lag, and I am not pretending I can beat it. Two weeks, three cities. Tokyo first, then Kyoto, then Osaka, and the itinerary is honestly quite tight. Here is the part I am proud of. I have been saving since February, a little every single week, and by the time we set off I will have put away enough for the trains and the food without asking my parents for anything. The flights were the problem. We are going in peak season, because school breaks do not move, so everything is more expensive and half the hostels were fully booked in March already. Three things I have learned from planning it. First, pack light, because you carry that bag through four subway stations and nobody helps you. Second, buy the transport card on the first morning, because it is the cheapest way to get around and you will use it eleven times a day. Third, leave one empty afternoon in every city. Every good thing that happened to my cousin out there happened on a detour, somewhere off the beaten track that was not in any plan. Anyway. By the time I see you in August I will have taken about four thousand photographs and you will have to sit through all of them. Talk soon.

First, fix the dates, because everything else on the list has a different price depending on the week you choose and nothing can be booked until those two days are decided. Then set the budget in a single number, since a plan that never names the amount is a wish, and the number is what tells you which of the next decisions are even possible. After that, book the flights, because they are the part that sells out first and the part that costs most if you wait. Next, build the itinerary city by city, and leave one empty afternoon in every city for the detour you cannot plan. Finally, work backwards from the departure date and write the deadline for every remaining task, so that by the time you set off there is nothing left on the list.
By July I will have saved enough for the flights.
We will not have finished the itinerary by Friday.
By the time we land, we will have been in the air for twenty-six hours.
Will you have booked the hostel by then?
By the time you wake up, I will already have packed.
I will have booked everything by Friday.
